items.title: NBER working paper 35275 — 'Writing Code vs. Shipping Code': the 0.25 AI-vs-human-effort elasticity now sits alongside Faros AI telemetry (PR volume +98%, PR review time +91%) and CircleCI's main-branch throughput down 7% / success at 70.8%
items.summary: An NBER working paper (number 35275, 'Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools' by Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, originally posted May 2026) has been the empirical anchor for the week's 'commits up, releases flat' debate, and the picture around it filled in further overnight. The paper's matched event study tracks AI usage telemetry across more than 100,000 GitHub developers and four app marketplaces. It estimates an elasticity of substitution of 0.25 between AI and human effort, which the authors read as strong complementarity — a 'weak-link' view in which human bottlenecks (chiefly code review and release engineering) cap how much AI's task-level speedups actually reach shipped software. On the marketplace half, they find a moderate increase in new apps shipped but no corresponding increase in total marketplace usage. The circulating this-week summaries disagree on the headline multipliers: a Product Hunt gloss headlines commits up ~240% / releases up ~30%, a July Codex-focused write-up gives commits +180% / releases +30% under autonomous agents, and a separate blog cites 741% more lines of code against only 20% more releases — the paper's own abstract wording is more cautious than any of these, so the 0.25 elasticity figure is the one worth filing and the headline multipliers are all re-glosses. Two independent datasets have come into the same frame since the paper landed: Faros AI telemetry across more than 10,000 developers shows PR merge volume up 98% and PR review time up 91% on high-adoption teams, while CircleCI's 2026 State of Software Delivery report has main-branch throughput down 7% for the median team and main-branch success at 70.8% — the lowest in more than five years. A LinearB 2026 benchmark, cited across multiple write-ups, puts the merge rate of AI-generated pull requests at 32.7% against roughly 84.5% for human-authored code, with the queue time before review 4.6x longer for AI PRs; a widely-circulated METR / LinearB result adds that developers perceive themselves ~20% faster while the measured delta is ~19% slower (confidence interval wide enough that the slowdown is not statistically significant on its own). A separate secondary claim — 61% of AI-agent pull requests reportedly receive no review at all — is a secondary write-up figure and not yet traced to a primary dataset.
items.why_it_matters: This is the clearest empirical read yet on a question every Python hobbyist starts to ask once they've used Claude Code, Cursor or an agent for a few weeks: 'OK, but is any of the extra code I'm writing actually making it into a shipped thing?' With the Faros, CircleCI, LinearB and METR datasets now stacked next to the NBER paper, the answer at labour-economics rigor is 'partially — and the limiting factor is your review-and-ship loop, not the model.' The 0.25 elasticity of substitution is the technical core: it says AI and human effort are closer to complements than substitutes in this data, which is the opposite of the 'AI replaces developers' framing most launch-day press runs with. The weak-link / human-bottleneck framing is also actionable: review speed, merge speed, test speed and the time it takes you yourself to agree the thing works are the things that most determine whether a day of agent-assisted writing turns into a release, and those are all human-side knobs. Four practical takeaways: (1) if you're using an AI coding tool and feel like you're generating a lot of code without shipping proportionally more features, the data says that is the median experience, not your personal failure — and the fix is not 'use the model more' but 'shorten your review-and-merge loop,' which for a solo hobbyist means things like better test coverage, smaller PR-sized changes, and a working CI that auto-runs on push; (2) the LinearB 32.7% vs 84.5% merge-rate gap is the number to file for anyone building agent-authored PRs into a workflow — AI-generated code is roughly 2.5x less likely to merge, so the pipeline needs to assume more rework, not less; (3) the Faros 'PR volume up 98%, PR review time up 91%' pair, combined with CircleCI's main-branch success falling to 70.8% (five-year low) and median throughput down 7%, is the live-data pattern — adoption is clearly real at the writing stage, but main-branch health is quietly degrading in parallel, which is the shape of the bottleneck in production; (4) the paper's finding of 'new apps up, total usage flat' on marketplaces is the honest shape of the Cambrian-explosion debate — more things are being built, but it is not obvious yet that users are consuming more of them. The broader read: the next phase of the agentic-coding story is not another model benchmark; it is tool and workflow design that collapses the review-and-ship bottleneck. Expect vendors (GitHub, Linear, Atlassian, agentic-review startups) to pile into exactly that gap over the next two quarters — AWS already framed the problem as 'review capacity, not developer output, is the limiting factor in delivery' back in March 2026, and the Winter '27 Agentforce rollout on an adjacent beat shows the enterprise-vendor response arriving. Also worth watching skeptically: the headline multipliers that circulate alongside this paper (240% / 180% / 741% commits, 20% / 30% releases) are all secondary glosses and they disagree with each other — the 0.25 elasticity is the primary figure.

items.title: Salesforce Winter '27 GA — Agentforce on by default across existing orgs, Agentic Commerce Search self-reports 13% conversion / 17% add-to-cart lift (metric inherited from Cimulate acquisition), PowerSchool cited at 550 users on Adaptive Experience in production
items.summary: Salesforce's Winter '27 product release reached general availability on Monday, October 12, 2026 — the first release in which Agentforce, Salesforce's AI-agent layer, runs entire multi-step workflows rather than only answering questions in-context. The release packages 15 'innovations' across contact center, commerce, scheduling, Slack integration, voice, and developer tooling, and lands on top of an Agentforce auto-enablement rollout that Salesforce began the first week of September (originally planned for August, then shifted to a rolling phase-in). On commerce, Salesforce credits the new Agentic Commerce Search feature with a 13% conversion lift and a 17% add-to-cart lift in early customer deployments — the technology came from Cimulate, which Salesforce acquired, and secondary analysis has pointed out that Salesforce's product-page footnotes attribute the metrics to Cimulate customer success data, so the measurement window, number of merchants, and baseline are not disclosed in the public announcement and the figures may inherit from pre-acquisition Cimulate deployments rather than new Salesforce production data. Analysts have accordingly flagged them as vendor-reported figures rather than independently audited ones. On financial services, Agentforce Financial Services (formerly Financial Services Cloud) is moving to customers' production orgs in upgrade windows on October 2, 9, and 10 ahead of today's GA. Marketing coverage highlights two new agents for campaign creation and lead nurturing, plus email-deliverability monitoring in Marketing Cloud Next and Account Engagement. Salesforce has also pointed to Adaptive Experience as a customer-cited anchor — PowerSchool with more than 550 users is running it in production. The release is the first Salesforce major-cycle where Agentforce is on by default for existing orgs rather than opt-in — a specific contractual and compliance change for customers in regulated industries that depend on explicit admin provisioning; Salesforce says the auto-enablement comes at no additional cost and with no billing change, and secondary analysis has argued this framing is also a description of a decision customers no longer get to make.
items.why_it_matters: Salesforce going agents-run-whole-workflows by default is the clearest 'agents are the business layer now' signal from an enterprise vendor the size of an enterprise vendor — it is the kind of release that quietly moves 'agents' from a demo category to a line item on IT budgets, because every mid-market company already paying for Salesforce now has agents running against their CRM data whether they explicitly opted in or not. For a hobbyist Python coder, the direct relevance is thin (you're not writing Apex), but the indirect read is useful in a few ways: (1) the auto-enablement model — rolling 'on by default' through existing customer orgs at no additional cost, with the framing that it is 'a decision you no longer get to make' — is the shape the next wave of SaaS-agent rollouts will take, and it is worth watching how customers in regulated industries react, because that reaction will set the compliance template every other vendor copies; (2) the 'Agentic Commerce Search → 13% conversion lift / 17% add-to-cart lift' claim is a specific example of the AI-feature-attribution problem that is going to dominate the next year of enterprise AI reporting — a vendor can report a lift against any baseline it chooses, and the Cimulate-acquisition provenance of the figure (metrics inherited from the acquired company's pre-acquisition customer success data) is a textbook case of why 'our feature lifted conversion X%' needs more sourcing than it usually gets; it is the right skeptical lens to apply to every 'AI increased X by Y%' number from a vendor's own press release, including Salesforce's; (3) the broader framing — 'agents run the workflow, not just answer in-context' — is the industry-wide positioning shift from the chat-interface era to the business-logic-execution era, and that is also where Python-stack projects (LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex Workflows, CrewAI, Microsoft AutoGen, OpenAI's Agent SDK) are competing with the enterprise suites. The practical thing to file: when a vendor the size of Salesforce ships 'agents on by default,' the ceiling for what's acceptable in agentic release engineering just moved — Salesforce has infrastructure, compliance, and support staff for 'oops the agent did the wrong thing,' and the startups shipping similar features into a hobbyist's own workflow mostly don't. Pick agentic tools with that asymmetry in mind. PowerSchool at 550 users on Adaptive Experience is the specific customer-cited anchor to watch — one real production reference beats ten press-release logos.
